prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic clocks to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep B015 (Katori, Ye) as a single-part prize and my position has not changed since round 1. After reading the full exchange, the case rests on three things that the other files do not contradict. First, the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea: it cancels the trap-induced light shift while keeping Lamb-Dicke confinement and many-atom averaging, which a single trapped ion cannot do, so it is a different architecture and not a tuned version of the 2012 ion work or of the 2005 comb. Second, the roles are separable: Katori proposed the concept and built the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group drove the accuracy and stability frontier to about 10^-18. Third, the result is mature and checkable, because lattice clocks in different laboratories and with different species agree at this level, and uses such as tests of constants and relativistic geodesy are already running. A citation worded around the lattice concept and its realisation, and not around combs or clocks in general, answers the novelty objection in the text itself. I treat the pending redefinition of the second as a metrology milestone decided elsewhere, not as a doubt about the physics.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) honoured the frequency comb and single-ion quantum control, and a member can fairly say the lattice clock is the next step in a line already rewarded. Two names also leave out real contributors, among them Lemonde at SYRTE, Lisdat at PTB, and the JILA co-workers (Ludlow, Bloom, Lemke, Hinkley), and Katori's concept and Ye's performance work are different kinds of contribution, so the credit is cleaner than for the other shortlisted candidates but not complete. Pearce is right that B014 opens a whole new observational window, and a committee that ranks breadth of discovery above attribution could reasonably choose it. I weigh clean credit and independent confirmation more heavily this year, but that is a judgement, not a measurable criterion.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B015 sixth and prefers B018 (Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan), arguing that band topology with a Z2 invariant is a new organising principle, while also conceding that Mele and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposers cannot fit in three names and that the 2016 prize touches neighbouring ground.
responses.response: I accept that topological insulators are a deep and mature idea, and I answer his novelty worry on B015 directly. The lattice clock differs from the single-ion clock in the physics that fixes accuracy: many atoms are interrogated at once in a lattice at the magic wavelength, so the light shift cancels while the atoms stay in the Lamb-Dicke regime. That separates it from both the comb and the ion work. What decides it for me is the credit that he himself says is the weak point of B018. With Mele and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang left out, and B003 offering Xue instead of Hasan, the committee would be choosing the third laureate arbitrarily, whereas the B015 credit follows a concept-and-realisation split that no file disputes. I would keep B018 as my second alternative, in case the committee wants a condensed-matter prize.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B014 (Halzen, Karle) as a discovery of nature in the plain sense, but states that B015 should be preferred if the committee judges clean attribution to outweigh breadth of discovery.
responses.response: I agree with the way he framed the choice, and his own concession is the reason I stay with B015. The diffuse flux is a real discovery and I regard it as confirmed in several IceCube channels. But the credit problem he names, a collaboration of hundreds with AMANDA and DUMAND as precursors, is not a detail: two names would be a simplification the citation has to defend, and the source evidence (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane) is still statistically modest. Independent confirmation from KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD is still maturing. I would therefore keep B014 as a strong candidate for a later year and as my first alternative this year, and would not put a diffuse-flux citation ahead of B015 now. If he can show that a citation limited to the diffuse flux has a credit structure the committee accepts, I would reconsider the order.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved to B015 but says honestly that B014 is stronger on opening a wholly new observational window, and he asks whether Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat and others have claims that two names cannot represent.
responses.response: I think his candour on B014 is right and I do not dismiss the point about a new window. On the credit question, the other groups did important work, but the two-name credit is defensible because the first idea and the first strontium lattice clock belong to Katori, and the accuracy frontier that the community uses as a benchmark belongs to Ye's group. Lisdat, Lemonde and others confirmed and extended the result, which supports its maturity, but they did not establish the concept. I would like the citation to say so plainly. Because he asks me to record my own position, I note that I do not rank B039 above B015 in this round, so I am not using my place on the committee to promote a field I lead.

responses.point: Kroll supports B015 as a compact, fair two-name credit continuing the line of precision spectroscopy, and he discloses a doctoral-period research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder with which Jun Ye is associated.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific case and I have the same view as in round 1 on the citation: it should be about the magic-wavelength lattice and its realisation. On his disclosure, I read it as background and not a tie to the credited names, and I would support the committee recording it, as the chair asks, without it changing the weight of his support. I would also say that it applies to my own disclosure in the same way: both should be noted and neither makes a reason to discount the case for B015, which does not depend on any one member.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a distinct architecture and not a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which can only be settled by the wording of the citation.
Whether two names fairly represent the experimental credit for the 10^-18 clocks when SYRTE, PTB, NIST and JILA co-workers also contributed.
Whether a decision on B015 should wait for the redefinition of the second, which I do not think it should.
Whether breadth of discovery (B014) should outweigh clean credit (B015) this year, which is a difference of judgement among the members.
My own distance from this field: I am a theorist in superconducting circuits, not in atomic clocks, so I lean on the experimental comparison data that others have described.
statement.conflict_note: My documented connections are to superconducting circuits and quantum computing. I direct WACQT at Chalmers, I succeeded Per Delsing in that role, Chalmers colleagues (Delsing, C. M. Wilson) and my frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum work in superconducting circuits and waveguide QED, and I presented the 2025 prize. These may require recusal on B039 and nearby circuit candidates, and I have not put B039 in my preferred configuration or in my alternatives. I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye or the other B015 candidates, nor to the B014 or B018 names, so I do not see a conflict for my preferred configuration. I support recording the disclosures of Kroll and myself formally.
